body:
Why satellite applications matter to Gujarat

Gujarat has extensive agricultural areas, rapidly developing settlements, important water resources and a long coastline along the Arabian Sea. Satellite communication and Earth observation can support different public needs across these settings.

The main advantage of satellite technology is that information can be transmitted or collected across large geographical areas. Its usefulness depends on converting that capability into reliable observations, communication services and decisions suited to local requirements.

Important space-related institutions in Gujarat

Space Applications Centre, Ahmedabad

The Space Applications Centre (SAC) is an ISRO centre located in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. It develops satellite payloads and works on applications involving communication, remote sensing and other space technologies.

Its work includes instruments used in communication satellites and sensors used for Earth observation. The centre also contributes to applications concerning agriculture, oceans, the atmosphere and natural resources.

SAC is an important Indian institution for satellite applications and payload development. It should not be confused with a satellite-launch site.

BISAG-N, Gandhinagar

BISAG-N stands for Bhaskaracharya National Institute for Space Applications and Geo-informatics. It is an autonomous scientific society under the Government of India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, with facilities in Gandhinagar.

BISAG-N works in satellite communication, remote sensing, GIS and other geospatial applications. Its activities include resource mapping, planning support, agricultural monitoring and disaster-related geographical information.

A GIS can combine satellite images with administrative, survey and infrastructure information. This allows satellite-derived observations to be interpreted in the geographical and administrative context in which decisions must be made.

Gujarat SATCOM Network and VANDE Gujarat

The Gujarat SATCOM Network uses satellite communication for activities such as distance education, training, skill development, agriculture-related information and public awareness.

VANDE Gujarat is associated with educational DTH television broadcasting using facilities at BISAG-N. This is a Gujarat example of a communication application, because information is transmitted to learners and other viewers.

BISAG-N's official satellite-communication information, consulted on 4 November 2026, describes VANDE Gujarat educational channels and the Gujarat SATCOM Network. Individual channel counts and service arrangements can change.

Remote sensing for Gujarat's land and water resources

Agricultural observation

Satellite observations can help assess crop distribution, vegetation condition and seasonal changes. For example, repeated images of cultivated areas in Gujarat can provide information about differences in vegetation cover between growing seasons.

Such observations can contribute to agricultural planning, but they do not automatically identify every cause of poor crop growth. Rainfall records, soil conditions, agricultural practices and field observations may also be necessary.

Water-resource management

Remote-sensing images can help map reservoirs, rivers, surface-water spread and land-cover changes affecting drainage. When combined with rainfall and other information, these observations can support water-resource assessment and planning.

Urban planning

Repeated detailed imagery can reveal changes in built-up areas around cities such as Ahmedabad and Surat. These observations can contribute to land-use mapping and infrastructure planning.

Satellite imagery supplies geographical evidence; it does not replace official survey records, land-use permissions or statutory planning procedures.

Gujarat's coastline and disaster preparedness

Weather monitoring over the Arabian Sea

Gujarat's Arabian Sea coastline makes cyclone monitoring and marine weather information especially relevant. Geostationary meteorological satellites provide repeated observations of cloud systems and weather developments over the Arabian Sea.

IMD combines satellite observations with other meteorological information to prepare forecasts and warnings. The warnings can then be communicated through appropriate public information and disaster-management channels.

Coastal and ocean observations

Oceansat-type observations provide information about ocean conditions, including ocean colour, temperature and surface winds. Such information can contribute to marine-resource studies and potential fishing-zone advisories.

Flood assessment and disaster response

Earth-observation satellites can help identify flooded areas by comparing observations from different dates. Radar satellites are particularly useful when monsoon cloud cover limits optical imaging.

Satellite-based mapping helps authorities understand the geographical extent of an event. Ground reports remain important for assessing damage, identifying immediate needs and determining the appropriate response.

National satellite-information services supporting states

ISRO's Disaster Management Support Programme

ISRO's Disaster Management Support (DMS) Programme uses space-based information to support disaster preparedness, assessment and response. It provides relevant information to central and state authorities.

Satellite observations can support different stages of disaster management, including identifying hazard-prone conditions, assessing affected areas and monitoring changes after an event.

Bhuvan and MOSDAC

Bhuvan is an NRSC geospatial platform that provides access to satellite-derived geographical information and thematic products.

MOSDAC, the Meteorological and Oceanographic Satellite Data Archival Centre, is a data centre of SAC, Ahmedabad. It supports the reception, processing, analysis and dissemination of meteorological and oceanographic satellite data.

The distinction is important: these are information services or facilities, not individual satellites. They help turn measurements made by satellites into information that users can access and interpret.

Choosing the appropriate satellite application

The first distinction is between sending information and collecting information about the Earth.

  • Sending a lesson to distant classrooms: This requires a communication service. INSAT, GSAT and educational satellite communication are relevant examples.
  • Mapping crops, forests, reservoirs or settlements: This requires Earth-observation information. Resourcesat and Cartosat are relevant Indian satellite families.
  • Observing ocean conditions: Oceansat missions provide relevant marine measurements.
  • Mapping flooded land under cloud cover: Radar Earth observation, including RISAT-type missions, is particularly useful.
  • Monitoring developing cyclones and cloud systems: Meteorological observations from INSAT-type weather satellites are useful, with forecasting performed using several sources of data.

Connecting observations to public decisions

Satellite applications often work together. During a developing cyclone over the Arabian Sea, a meteorological satellite may provide cloud observations. IMD analyses observations and prepares a forecast or warning. Communication systems distribute the information. Earth-observation satellites may subsequently help map affected areas, while ground teams confirm conditions and carry out the response.

This illustrates why communication satellites, weather satellites and other Earth-observation satellites are complementary rather than interchangeable.

Prelims focus

  • SAC is an ISRO centre located in Ahmedabad.
  • BISAG-N stands for Bhaskaracharya National Institute for Space Applications and Geo-informatics and has facilities in Gandhinagar.
  • VANDE Gujarat is associated with educational DTH broadcasting through BISAG-N facilities.
  • NRSC's Bhuvan provides geospatial information services.
  • MOSDAC is associated with SAC and meteorological and oceanographic satellite data.
  • Trap: SAC, BISAG-N, Bhuvan and MOSDAC are institutions or information facilities, not satellite names.
